unit-01.description: The language and its rules. Before a single gate is described, you need the design flow, the vocabulary of HDL-based design, the module as a unit of hierarchy, and the data model that every later construction depends on.
objectives: Trace a design from specification to silicon and identify where Verilog enters the flow.
Compare Verilog with VHDL and place each modelling style on the abstraction ladder.
Build and connect module hierarchies with correct port directions and widths.
Use literals, nets, variables, vectors, arrays, parameters and system tasks correctly.
Evaluate expressions with Verilog's width, signedness and precedence rules.

unit-02.description: Structural and dataflow modelling. Describe hardware as a netlist of primitive gates or as continuous equations over signals, then assemble the arithmetic and routing blocks that make up a datapath.
objectives: Instantiate gate primitives and model rise, fall and turn-off delays.
Write continuous assignments that describe combinational hardware without inferred storage.
Build adders, subtractors, comparators, multiplexers, decoders and encoders.
Choose between gate-level, dataflow and behavioural descriptions for a given block.

unit-03.description: Behavioural modelling. Procedural blocks describe what hardware does over time. This unit covers the event model, assignment scheduling, timing controls, decision constructs, loops, block structure and custom primitives.
objectives: Distinguish initial from always, and blocking from non-blocking assignments.
Use delay, event and wait controls, and know which controls synthesis ignores.
Write conditionals, case statements and loops that synthesise predictably.
Explain sequential and parallel blocks, and define combinational and sequential UDPs.

vlsi-design-flow.summary: Follow a design from specification to silicon, and see exactly where RTL, simulation, synthesis and verification fit in the VLSI flow.

vhdl-vs-verilog.summary: Compare the two dominant hardware description languages, then place Verilog's modelling styles on the abstraction ladder.

modules-instances-ports.summary: Treat a module as a hardware component: declare its ports, connect instances by name, and avoid the direction and width errors that break elaboration.

hierarchical-modelling.summary: Compose verified leaf cells into larger designs, and choose between top-down, bottom-up and mixed design methods.

lexical-conventions.summary: Read and write Verilog's identifiers, comments, literals and sized numbers without ambiguity.

data-types.summary: Understand nets, variables, vectors and the four-valued logic that Verilog actually simulates.

arrays-memories-strings.summary: Distinguish a vector from an array, model memories correctly, and store text without borrowing SystemVerilog types.

parameters.summary: Make modules reusable with parameters, override them deliberately, and protect internal constants with localparam.

system-tasks-directives.summary: Use simulation tasks and compiler directives deliberately, and keep them out of synthesizable hardware.

expressions-operators.summary: Learn how Verilog sizes, signs and evaluates expressions, and why operator precedence alone is not enough.

gate-primitives.summary: Instantiate primitive gates, read their truth tables, and know when gate-level modelling is the right level of detail.

gate-delays.summary: Model rise, fall and turn-off delays, and interpret the simulator's timing results instead of guessing them.

dataflow-modelling.summary: Describe combinational hardware as continuous equations, and recognise when an assignment describes a latch by accident.

adders-subtractors-comparators.summary: Build arithmetic and comparison hardware, and keep unsigned carry-out separate from signed overflow.

mux-demux-encoder-decoder.summary: Implement the selection, routing and encoding blocks that sit inside almost every datapath.

alu-modelling-comparison.summary: Design a small ALU, then compare gate-level, dataflow and behavioural descriptions of the same function.

initial-always.summary: Use Verilog's two procedural constructs for their real purposes: one-shot setup and synthesizable repeated behaviour.

blocking-nonblocking.summary: See why blocking and non-blocking assignments produce different hardware, and where each one belongs.

timing-controls.summary: Control when statements execute with delays, events and waits, and know which controls synthesis ignores.

conditionals-case.summary: Choose between if/else, case, casez and casex, and avoid the latches and masked bugs they can introduce.

loops.summary: Use for, while, repeat and forever loops correctly in simulation and in synthesizable hardware.

sequential-parallel-blocks.summary: Understand statement ordering inside begin/end and true concurrency inside fork/join.

udp.summary: Define custom primitive gates with truth tables, including edge-triggered sequential primitives.
